critic.verdict: Film is coherent and era-appropriate but its reveal is too timid to publish; plate itself is clean.

rounds.verdict: Do not publish as rendered: the reveal concept fits the scene, but a single-player cut-out breaking from the row and an accordion floating off its chair make the motion incoherent, and neither end frame is a clean plate.
filmIssues: The pull-back reveal is the right idea but reads timidly in the sheet: t=0 is not convincingly tight on the accordion and t=1 still feels cropped rather than arriving on the full printed plate, so neither the opening nor the held final picture is strong.

cut-1 ('players') is only one figure from the right-hand part of the row, not the whole row. With depth 0.6 and drift it separates from the painted players beside it, appearing conspicuously smaller / out of register with its neighbours and breaking the united line of the troupe in every frame.

cut-2 is the accordion alone, but the chair it rests on stays in the background. Its drift, 1.02 scale and higher depth let it slide and grow against that fixed chair, creating a doubled / floating edge and making the accordion detach from its support.

Side folding chairs and music stands are awkwardly clipped at the frame edges throughout, especially at t=0 and t=1, and the final frame is not a clean, centred full-plate picture to dwell on while reading.
Halftone-shimmer is fitting and subtle for the 1970s silkscreen style, and the era's print texture is otherwise preserved.

filmIssues: The intended pull-back reveal is legible but timid: at t=0 the 1.30 zoom already shows all five players and most of the room, so there is little discovery as it settles to the full plate — it reads close to a plain slow zoom rather than a story-telling reveal.

The opening frame clips the side folding chairs awkwardly at both edges without being tight enough on the accordion to justify the crop; the final full-plate frame is, by contrast, a good dwell picture.

Subject coherence is good: the cut-out player stays locked in the painted row and the accordion stays on its front chair, with no tearing, doubling, halo or visible ghost in the frames, and the halftone-shimmer is fitting and subtle for the 1970s silkscreen style.
